What the person did: A coworker altered a photo of a female sheriff's deputy so she appeared in uniform with her breasts exposed, then showed and e-mailed it to others for about ten months.

Fact pattern: Fabricated video, audio, images, quotes, or factual claims that put real people in a false light (political and propaganda deepfakes, doctored photos, invented quotes, AI-generated false accusations about named people)

Court: Supreme Court of the United States
What the person did: A newspaper reporter published a feature story about a widow and her family that invented details, including describing her demeanor during a visit at which she was not present.
Outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Sixth Circuit and reinstated the jury's false-light verdict and compensatory damages against the reporter and the publisher (respondeat superior); the verdict against the photographer was not reinstated.

How the facts compare: Cantrell holds a writer liable in false light for presenting invented facts about real people as true, which is what fabricated quotes (incidents 764, 1392, 1504) do directly and what political deepfakes do in audio or video form. Public-figure targets must show knowing or reckless falsity, as the Cantrell jury was instructed; for AI-generated false accusations (770, 1205, 1334) see the defamation file for AI-specific rulings.

Fact pattern: Tracking a specific person's movements or location for personal reasons (officers misusing license-plate-reader and police databases to follow exes and partners, GPS trackers)
Court: U.S. District Court, E.D. Pennsylvania
What the person did: Television journalists engaged in a course of following, filming, and hounding a family at their homes and elsewhere.

How the facts compare: Wolfson supports intrusion liability for sustained surveillance of a person even in public, which is what officers did when they ran hundreds of plate searches to follow an estranged spouse or ex (and in 1705 also followed her in a patrol car; in 1706 planted a GPS tracker). Courts treat faces shown in public as not secluded, and employer or school monitoring of their own systems is usually justified or consented to, so no decision holding a person or company liable under Restatement 652B-652E for this kind of institutional monitoring turned up. Government actors (76, 249, 531, 659, 829, 1075) would also raise sovereign-immunity barriers; constitutional and biometric-statute claims are the usual vehicles.

Fact pattern: Police stopping and holding innocent drivers and families at gunpoint on unverified plate-reader or database hits
Court: California Court of Appeal, Second District, Division Four (No. B090764)
What the person did: A state investigator executing a warrant pointed out the wrong man without comparing him to the suspect's photo she carried, and officers seized him in a painful restraint and refused to check the identification he offered until they reached his car.
Outcome: Court of Appeal held the false arrest claim had to go to the jury: the seizure was an arrest, and the evidence showed no reasonable basis to believe he was the man named in the warrant; the directed-verdict denial was upheld and the order granting him a new trial affirmed.
Quote (verified text): There is ample evidence that the State appellants lacked a reasonable basis to conclude that respondent was the man they sought.
How the facts compare: Bell turns on the failure in the plate-reader stops: officers seized and restrained someone on a mismatch they could have caught by checking information already in hand. City and County of San Francisco, 751 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2014) (incident 245's own stop), both read via Midpage, are federal Fourth Amendment analogs; neither decided a state false imprisonment claim. A brief stop on a database hit can be privileged if the officer had reasonable suspicion, so liability turns on ignoring readily available mismatches.
Later treatment: Not reversed; review denied July 29, 1998. Midpage: Caution, no negative (85 citing refs); the caution entries concern its juror-misconduct and new-trial rulings (Romo v. What the person did: Two New York City Transit Police officers arrested minority men on subway trains for sexual abuse that the purported victims said had not happened, writing reports that victims had complained and would press charges; Count Four charged the false arrest of Orrett Hall, a non-citizen resident, under § 242.

Quote (verified text): when police officers acting in bad faith make an arrest without probable cause, the person arrested has suffered a deprivation of liberty without due process of law
